analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing customers and workers into arbitration before disputes happen.
analysis.headline: The House passed the FAIR Act 225-186 in September 2019, but the Senate never voted on it, so forced arbitration clauses remain enforceable.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of workers and consumers sign contracts — for jobs, credit cards, bank accounts, nursing homes, and software — that require any dispute to be resolved in private arbitration instead of court, and bar them from joining class actions. The FAIR Act would void those clauses for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes. People could still choose arbitration voluntarily after a dispute arises, and union contracts are untouched. The House passed it, but the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers with arbitration clauses in their employment or purchase contracts. They could sue in court, join class actions, and appeal — instead of private arbitration where decisions are largely secret, appeal is rarely available, and class claims are usually banned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers facing forced arbitration

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, letting people take those cases to court [S2][S5].
It also voids clauses that waive the right to participate in a joint, class, or collective action, restoring access to the class actions that make small-value claims worth litigating [S5].
Arbitration remains available when both sides choose it after a dispute arises, and union-negotiated arbitration under collective bargaining agreements is preserved [S5].
Whether the law applies is decided by a court rather than an arbitrator, closing the loophole where companies send even the challenge to the clause itself to the arbitrator [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that currently rely on forced arbitration — employers, banks, credit card issuers, nursing homes, and other consumer businesses — would face court litigation and class actions they now funnel into private arbitration, plus the associated legal costs.

drawbacks.text: Court litigation is slow and expensive; for individual claims too small to justify a lawyer, arbitration can be a faster, cheaper route than a solo court case, and the bill would not create a substitute for it [S5].
Businesses would bear higher litigation costs from employment and consumer suits, which critics said could be passed on to consumers in prices [S7].
The bill reaches new claims only; it applies to disputes arising after enactment, so existing arbitration clauses would remain valid for past conduct [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill removes a structural disadvantage: when a company wrongs many people a little at a time, forced arbitration plus class waivers leaves almost no one able to pursue a remedy. The cost is more litigation for business, and the strongest honest objection is that some individuals with small claims might prefer arbitration to an empty court docket. On balance the benefit of restoring collective legal rights outweighs that cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it, but the Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended without ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill 22-14 on September 13, 2019 [S7].
The House passed the FAIR Act on September 20, 2019 by 225-186, with 223 of 234 voting Democrats in favor and 2 of 199 voting Republicans in favor [S8][S7].
The Senate received the bill on September 24, 2019 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; no further action followed before the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S7].
The House bill had 222 cosponsors, 221 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that write forced arbitration clauses — employers, banks, and consumer businesses — kept their ability to route disputes into private arbitration and block class actions. Consumers and workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that use forced arbitration clauses

industries.industry: Employers and consumer-facing businesses (banks, credit card issuers, telecom, nursing homes)
industries.note: These companies rely on predispute arbitration clauses to move disputes out of court and block class actions; the bill would void those clauses, exposing them to lawsuits and class litigation. Their interest in keeping the clauses runs against the court access of their workers and customers.

Mandatory arbitration in consumer and employment contracts is the core of their business volume; the bill keeps arbitration only as a voluntary post-dispute choice, shrinking the market the clauses create.
Restoring court access and class actions expands the kinds of cases that can be litigated, and class actions are the mechanism through which many small-value claims reach the public's hands.
